### 2026-10-11 – # ProcrastiNoT — From a Study Problem to a Two-Device Hardware Design

**6h**

# ProcrastiNoT — From a Study Problem to a Two-Device Hardware Design

My first six hours on ProcrastiNoT were mostly about understanding the problem, researching existing solutions, and figuring out what I would actually need to build before starting the PCB design.

I didn't want to jump straight into choosing components and drawing circuits without understanding what the project was supposed to achieve. The challenge was turning a broad idea—helping students study in a better environment—into a realistic system with specific features, sensors, and hardware requirements.

## Hour 1 — Researching the problem and defining the features

I started by researching the problem that ProcrastiNoT is intended to address. My goal is to create an ideal studying environment that minimizes distractions while keeping the student aware of the task they're working on, the time remaining for that task, and the larger goal they are working toward.

I initially used broad search queries, including **"most common study problems for students and how to tackle them"** and **"what are the distractions that prevent students from focusing on their studies."** I took notes in my notebook while going through this research.

![Figure 1: My notebook notes from the initial problem research](PASTE-FIGURE-1-IMAGE-URL-HERE)
![Figure 1](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/IOQCx0uhKFahh6D6pbHCyLi6M0WpGnDR/d5b96ed083000fb74663e09d1db23a7d22747b5360111c1d45bd46fff016fb78.jpg)
After that, I sketched a rough idea of the features I wanted. I also used ChatGPT to help me evaluate how different features could contribute to the main goal and identify existing projects worth investigating instead of spending hours searching through unrelated projects on Instructables.

Two projects I investigated were [Smart-Study-Desk](https://github.com/DukeDamaz/Smart-Study-Desk) and [ESP32 Smart Desk System](https://github.com/dasha-dotcom/smart-desk).

I looked at how these projects approached study-time tracking and presence detection. Comparing existing implementations helped me think more concretely about how my own device should detect the student's presence and keep track of a study session.

By the end of this hour, I had developed a more concrete feature list for ProcrastiNoT, shown in Figure 2.

![Figure 2: My initial feature list for ProcrastiNoT](PASTE-FIGURE-2-IMAGE-URL-HERE)
![Figure 2](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/IOQCx0uhKFahh6D6pbHCyLi6M0WpGnDR/427e0935c4e966b97446ef35ad8dd59287cb2a19a139c9ae0eb47e68fe195715.jpg)

## Hour 2 — Reconsidering presence detection and expanding the design

After analyzing existing solutions, I started refining my feature sketches and identifying the materials I would need before beginning the PCB design.

One important design decision concerned presence detection. My initial approach depended on an ultrasonic sensor. However, while investigating existing implementations and sensor documentation, I became concerned that the sensor's mounting direction and detection area would constrain where it could be installed. The student might change their seating position or decide to study somewhere else, such as on a bed, so I didn't want the physical placement of the sensor to unnecessarily limit the system.

I therefore shifted my design toward the **HLK-LD2410C millimeter-wave radar presence sensor**.

I examined the module's documentation to understand its dimensions, interfaces, and integration requirements. Its compact rectangular form factor, approximately 16 × 22 mm, looked promising for a PCB-based design. I also checked its logic interface and supply requirements to understand how it could connect to the Raspberry Pi 5, which I had selected as the main computing board.

[HLK-LD2410C manufacturer documentation](https://www.hlktech.com/en/Goods-239.html)

![Figure 4: HLK-LD2410C presence sensor and its documentation](PASTE-FIGURE-4-IMAGE-URL-HERE)
![Figure 4](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/IOQCx0uhKFahh6D6pbHCyLi6M0WpGnDR/725da2f1802ddcf4041922af1701b6f60b8fa669e4e9dbc6b0fc704cd0c726c6.jpg)

While refining the design, I also considered the screen, buzzer, and LEDs needed to communicate the device's current state to the student.

I then came up with an additional idea: a custom wearable band that would keep the student informed about their break, the day's tasks, the current time, and how many minutes they had exceeded their permitted break.

This significantly changed the project scope. Instead of designing only one stationary device, I now had **two connected hardware systems to plan for**: a desk-based device and a wearable device. Each would require its own PCB design, along with a way for the two systems to work together.

![Figure 3: My refined feature sketch showing the developing system Components](PASTE-FIGURE-3-IMAGE-URL-HERE)

![Figure 3](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/IOQCx0uhKFahh6D6pbHCyLi6M0WpGnDR/cdbcbaa293f8468ed2f29a18f7f0d2e08c015667d387a0e9660946f79445444c.jpg)
## Hour 3 — Comparing components and building the BOM

With the two-device concept becoming clearer, I began investigating potential components in more detail.

I compared different parts, looked at their prices through store websites, and checked their compatibility using component documentation and review videos. I wanted to avoid selecting parts merely because they looked suitable individually; they also needed to make sense within the overall system.

I started organizing the component information into a Bill of Materials (BOM), including the parts I would need and potential places to purchase them.

At this point, I was still evaluating the components rather than treating every choice as final. I needed a more complete understanding of their compatibility and availability before committing to a PCB design.

## Hour 4 — Investigating the AI component and computing requirements

Next, I focused on the AI aspect of ProcrastiNoT.

One of the problems I wanted to investigate was a limitation that simple presence detection cannot solve: if a student is sitting at their desk and has studying-related tabs open on their laptop, that does not necessarily mean they are actually studying.

I began researching AI models that might help address this problem. My goal was to understand how these models work and what computational resources they require, so that I could make a more informed decision about the computing platform needed for this feature, I've also tried one of the awesome avaliable online projects on https://local-eye-tracking.vercel.app/, Shown on Figure 5.

![Figure 5 : Me while Trying The old AI Project](PASTE-FIGURE-3-IMAGE-URL-HERE)
![Figure 5](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/IOQCx0uhKFahh6D6pbHCyLi6M0WpGnDR/6d3292bd759efc59b41fd10deea2919f97d3bb5cb503fc3c60122ad91e850393.png)

This was important because I didn't want to choose the hardware without considering the AI workload I might eventually need to run.

I also reviewed the Starbie files to understand their format and submission requirements. Looking through its PCB-related files gave me a reference for how another project had organized its board design, which I could use to orient myself before creating my own.

## Hour 5 — Continuing the BOM and researching PCB fabrication

My notes for the beginning of this hour are incomplete, so I cannot reliably reconstruct every activity I performed during that part of the session.

The work I can account for is continuing to develop the BOM and researching options for getting custom-printed PCBs manufactured in Egypt.

Since I was planning two hardware devices, sourcing components and understanding the local PCB fabrication process were important practical considerations. I needed to consider not only what I could design electronically, but also how I could eventually obtain the boards and components needed to build the project.

## Hour 6 — Reviewing the BOM and learning PCB design fundamentals

During the sixth hour, I continued revising and reviewing the BOM to make the component list more organized before moving further into the PCB design process.

I also started learning the essentials of PCB design. I wanted to understand the design process and the basic considerations involved before translating my component choices into an actual board.

At this stage, I had made progress in defining the project, identifying the main hardware systems, investigating presence detection, researching component options, and preparing the BOM. However, the research and component-selection work were not the same as having a completed schematic or a manufacturing-ready PCB. I still needed to validate the final component choices and turn the design into an actual circuit.

![Figure 6: My Final BOM List ScreenShot](PASTE-FIGURE-3-IMAGE-URL-HERE)

![Figure 6](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/IOQCx0uhKFahh6D6pbHCyLi6M0WpGnDR/39499f307909c3f9c18853ed37bd77ccc17266783036d213a6cdf0cf822c3aad.png)

**The next step:** Continue learning the PCB workflow, validate the components and their electrical requirements, and begin translating the hardware plan into a KiCad schematic.

**TL;DR:** I spent my first six hours turning ProcrastiNoT from a broad study-support idea into a more concrete two-device system, researching existing projects and presence sensors, investigating the AI requirements, building and reviewing the BOM, and beginning to prepare for PCB design.

**Time spent this session: 6 hours.**
